cybersecurity_L1_003.notes: Ground truth B is well-supported by multiple independent sources. IEEE 2030.5 mandates: (1) HTTPS with TLS 1.2 (or higher) for all communications; (2) PKI-based mutual device authentication; (3) X.509 certificates issued through a three-tier CA hierarchy (SERCA → MCA → MICA); (4) role-based access concepts (client/server hierarchy, differentiating read vs. control commands); and (5) certificate revocation processes. One secondary source (dersec.io) cites TLS 1.3 as the current required version — the standard has evolved from its original TLS 1.2 mandate — but this does not contradict B, since answer B says "TLS 1.2" and is the historically correct and widely cited requirement. The distractors (A: optional TLS + symmetric keys; C: IPsec + MAC addresses; D: AES-256 app-layer + no PKI) are clearly inconsistent with the standard's mandatory PKI/TLS architecture. No exact verbatim match of the question text was found online, ruling out direct data contamination. The candidate sources listed in the task file include the actual IEEE 2030.5 standard (paywalled, not independently fetched) and NERC CIP/NIST SP 800-82 (not directly relevant to this specific question) — the supporting evidence comes from secondary analysis sources that accurately summarize the standard.

cybersecurity_L1_001.notes: The verbatim question text ("Describe the scope of NERC CIP standards CIP-002 through CIP-011. For each standard, provide a one-sentence summary of what it covers.") yielded only general NERC CIP reference pages in the contamination search — no exact or paraphrase match to benchmark-specific content, so contamination_signal=not_found. Three independent fetched sources corroborate the ground truth: CIP-002 requires identification and categorization of BES Cyber Systems by impact level (high/medium/low); CIP-003 covers security management controls; CIP-004 covers personnel and training; CIP-005 covers electronic security perimeters; CIP-006 covers physical security; CIP-007 covers system security management; CIP-008 covers incident reporting and response planning; CIP-009 covers recovery plans; CIP-010 covers configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-011 covers information protection. The Industrial Defender source provides nearly verbatim purpose statements from the official NERC standards text. The NERC official page (nerc.com/standards/reliability-standards/cip) and the CIP-002-5.1a PDF both returned HTTP 403, so direct official-document verification was blocked, but the secondary sources quote the official purpose language faithfully. Status set to verified because fetched quotes strongly support both the question's framing and the ground-truth answer.

cybersecurity_L1_004.notes: All four sources independently confirm the CIA-to-AIC priority inversion (Confidentiality > Integrity > Availability in IT vs Availability > Integrity > Confidentiality in OT) and the specific reasons why IT security practices are problematic in OT/power-system environments: legacy systems, unavailability of maintenance windows, risk of cascading physical failures from patching or isolating controllers, protocol incompatibility, and the outsized consequence of availability loss (grid outages vs. data loss).
